Seville
suh-VIL
n. (the Andalusian see of Isidore and of the Protestant congregation of San Isidoro del Campo destroyed in the autos of 1559 and 1560)
From Latin Hispalis through Arabic Ishbiliyah, the modern Spanish Sevilla.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Seville is the chief city of Andalusia and from 1503 held the monopoly of the American trade, which made it for a century the richest port in Europe. Its oldest claim is Isidore, archbishop from about 600, whose Etymologies preserved classical learning for the medieval West and whose Sentences taught the Visigothic church; he presided at the fourth council of Toledo in 633. Its sharpest claim is the congregation at the Hieronymite monastery of San Isidoro del Campo outside the city, which in the fifteen-fifties read evangelical books brought in by Julian Hernandez; the prior, Garcia Arias, and about a dozen monks fled in 1557, among them Casiodoro de Reina and Cipriano de Valera. The autos of September 1559 and December 1560 and the subsequent prosecutions ended the movement. The dictionary records Seville as a city that gave the church a great encyclopaedist and then burned its own best readers of the Bible, and notes that the two facts belong to the same institution five centuries apart.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines an etymology as the derivation of a word; a monopoly as the sole power of trade; a monastery as a house for religious persons; an auto is not in Webster, but a sentence is a judgment pronounced; and constancy as firmness of mind.

expand to see more

ETYMOLOGY, n. That part of philology which explains the origin and derivation of words, with a view to ascertain their radical or primary signification.

MONOPOLY, n. The sole power of vending any species of goods, obtained either by engrossing the articles in market or by a license from authority.

MONASTERY, n. A house of religious retirement, or of seclusion from ordinary temporal concerns; a convent; an abbey.

SENTENCE, n. A judgment pronounced by a court or judge upon a criminal; a determination or decision given.

CONSTANCY, n. Fixedness; firmness of mind; steadiness; perseverance in a purpose or opinion.

Modern Corruption

Andalusian see of Isidore and of the San Isidoro del Campo congregation, destroyed in the autos of 1559 and 1560 after its prior and monks had fled.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is the use of learning as a credential for an institution that will not be taught. Seville produced Isidore, who gathered everything the ancient world knew and handed it forward, and nine hundred years later the same see tried, condemned and burned a body of monks whose offence was reading. The dictionary draws the conclusion without softening it: a church may be the custodian of civilisation and still kill its own best students. What was taken from Seville went abroad and became a Bible, which is the pattern Luke records: “Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover, which is the measure of victory. John gives it in terms that do not require survival, “they loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11), and locates those killed in the place no record can reach, “I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God” (Rev 6:9). Paul writes from prison about the single thing in the cell that is not in custody, “but the word of God is not bound” (2Ti 2:9). The Spanish Bible that two of those fugitives produced is still printed and still read, which is a longer sentence than the tribunal passed.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek martyria (G3141), testimony; Greek diaspeiro (G1289), to scatter abroad; Greek thusiasterion (G2379), an altar.

expand to see more

Greek agapao (G0025) — to love, to set affection on; “they loved not their lives unto the death”, Revelation 12:11.

Greek diaspeiro (G1289) — to scatter abroad, to disperse; “they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word”, Acts 8:4.

Greek deo (G1210) — to bind, to chain; “but the word of God is not bound”, 2 Timothy 2:9.

Greek thusiasterion (G2379) — an altar, a place of sacrifice; “I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain”, Revelation 6:9.

Greek martyria (G3141) — a testimony borne; “and for the testimony which they held”, Revelation 6:9.

Usage

"“they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4) — what Seville's fugitives did."

"“they loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11) — the measure that does not require survival."

"“but the word of God is not bound” (2Ti 2:9) — the longer sentence."
